why: Nothing in the prose reads as non-native or machine-seamed: no calques, no agreement slips, consistent register, and the domain vocabulary is right (mixed-flow towers with inverted-V ducts, cross-flow columns, drying priced per ton per point of moisture, elevator deduction schedules, 'writes coverage' for an insurer). The friction is density, not error.

One sentence made me reread: 'A mixed-flow costs enough that it goes to operations drying for their neighbors as well as themselves, at so much per ton per point of moisture, and those operations run late and shut down hot.' Two ellipses in one sentence - 'costs enough that it goes to' standing in for 'is bought by', and the idiomatic 'at so much per X' rate construction. A strong Swedish candidate will get there, a mid-band one may stall.

Smaller idiom snags for a Swedish reader: 'the weak joint in the argument' (usual collocation is weak link/weak point; it works here because the register is mechanical), 'across the table from', and 'shut down hot'.

The four surnames - Calverend, Grendisham, Steadgrove, Ockendale - are all coined-sounding and cluster together with no ordinary name among them. Harmless to a student, but it is the one place the piece feels manufactured rather than reported.

The argument itself is genuinely well-built. Calverend's two findings (dirt, clock), Grendisham's precise rebuttal (the log's second timestamp is a call time, i.e. when somebody noticed, not when anything caught), and Steadgrove's re-sort by date are all distinct positions, and the alliances are non-trivial: Steadgrove agrees with Calverend on cleaning while rejecting the shutdown, which correctly puts him opposite Grendisham. Paragraph 5 adjudicates without overreaching.

Paragraph 5's claim that 'nobody in the argument now defends it on the old ground' is correct but subtle: Grendisham does still defend fines as a cause, she just shifts from 'mixed-flow ducts hold more' to 'a September swab does not capture February accumulation'. The distinction is real and the sentence survives it, but a careful reader has to hold both readings for a beat.

Reads as a genuine piece of writing: a British allotment-society vignette organised around one clear idea — the written rules (no inheritance, second refusal demotes you) versus what actually moves the list (people stopping, and quiet local discretion). The title pays off in paragraph 3 with the inherited rhubarb crowns.

All five gaps sit on strong fixed collocations or idioms and are solvable from local context without guesswork: 'take the long view' (1), 'Strictly, ...' in the 'strictly speaking / as written' sense reinforced by the next sentence 'That is the clause as written' (2), the set idiom 'dead men's shoes' (3), the 'not approving, but not ___ either' antonym frame that only 'censorious' completes (4), and 'the rule has not been invoked' (5).

Main friction: the final paragraph welds two unrelated vignettes together with no transition. It moves from the eighties tenant and her nephew straight into 'One name has stood at the top since 2019' in the same paragraph. I re-read to check I had not missed a connection; a paragraph break would fix it.

Minor friction: 'twelve years from a key' uses 'key' as a metonym for a plot before the gate or the hut key has been established for the reader — the meaning arrives a beat late. Same for 'It is simply not what the list runs on', where 'It' refers back to the clause across two sentences.
Arithmetic holds well enough to not distract: 58 names at 4-7 plots a year gives roughly 8-14 years, so 'twelve years' is a defensible figure for the secretary to quote rather than a slip.

Distractors are clean on a cold read. Nothing in the wrong options is quietly defensible: 'Curiously' (2) is actively contradicted by 'nobody disputes it or finds it odd'; 'gracious'/'cautious'/'anxious' (4) all sit on the wrong side of the 'not approving, but ... either' contrast; 'evoked' (5) is the classic near-miss for 'invoked' and is clearly wrong with a rule as object.

Cold-solved A in one pass. The text states plainly that height is 'the part worth reading' and that 'the pot that stands a course above its neighbours belongs to a flue that smoked' — a smoking flue is one drawing badly, so A is a direct restatement. B is contradicted (the narrowed mouth is given a draught reason, not rain/birds); C is contradicted by 'Pattern tells you very little'; D is contradicted by 'the pots seldom match' plus the builders'-yard/stock explanation.

The passage holds together as an argument: pattern is noise (three reasons given — stock, ornament, rebuilds), height is signal, and the closing mortar detail explains why a raised pot is a cheap thing to have tried. Voice is consistent essayistic British prose throughout.

Friction 1 — spatial wording: 'Behind each is a separate flue dropping to its own grate.' A flue is beneath a pot, not behind it. Viewed from across the road it is just about defensible as the observer's-eye sense, but 'under each' is what the sentence wants, and I re-read the clause to be sure I had the geometry right.

Friction 2 — terminology: pots are bedded in 'a fillet of mortar'. The standard British term for the mortar weathering around a chimney pot is flaunching; 'fillet' names the mortar at a roof abutment. Comprehensible, and it does not affect the answer, but it is the one word where the otherwise very assured trade register slips.

Friction 3 — loose causal claim: 'Narrowing the mouth helps as well, since the same gases leave faster through less of an opening.' Tapered pots really do improve draught (higher exit velocity, less downdraught), so the conclusion is sound, but the stated reason is a bare continuity argument that on its own would equally suggest added resistance. A physics-minded candidate may pause here. It sits outside the keyed content, so it costs nothing on the question.

Factual spot-checks that came out clean: the shortest flue on a stack is the attic one (it starts highest and all flues terminate together), and the shortest hot-gas column does give the weakest lift — the stated mechanism is correct, not decorative. An attic-bedroom fireplace in a terrace is period-plausible. 'A course above its neighbours' is used correctly for a brickwork layer.

Cold solve: the chandler's hatch was open 7am-8pm (13 hours) for 412 letters; the bookseller's 2pm-8pm (6 hours) for 390. Rather more than double the hours bought 22 extra letters, and both shut at the same moment the evening cart went. The only thing the two houses share is the cart's hour, so the volume tracks the cart, not the length of opening. D.

With the passage, B and C are flatly contradicted: 412 vs 390 is not 'far more', and the text says 'Both shut when the evening cart went at eight', so the bookseller did not stay open after the cart. A ascribes a motive ('stretched their opening hours in order to earn more') that the text never supplies, and it says 'the keepers' plural while only one of the two kept long hours - the bookseller's six-hour day is the opposite of stretching. The threepence-an-hour detail is the bait for A: it makes hour-padding thinkable, but the passage reports no intent and the surveyor noticed only a broken spring.

OPTION-ONLY ELIMINATION (no passage, wording alone). B and D are near-contradictories on the same variable: B asserts that longer opening produced far more letters, D asserts that opening length did not govern letter volume. A test-wise candidate takes the contradictory pair to contain the key and discards A and C. A is further discardable as the only option asserting an unobservable motive ('in order to earn'), and C as the only option that talks about one shop when the stem asks about 'the two receiving houses' - both read as detail-level claims rather than answers to an 'implied' stem. That leaves B/D, i.e. 50% without reading. From there the standard heuristic that an 'implied' answer is the counterintuitive one rather than the expected proportionality points at D. So option-only reasoning gets a well-drilled candidate from 25% to 50% deterministically and probably better than that heuristically. It does not reach the key with certainty - only the numbers 412/390 decide which half of the B/D pair is true - so I did not log this as a blocker, but the narrowing is real and worth the escalation's attention.

Reader check on the facts: nothing rang false. Pillar boxes postdate 1846 in Britain, so 'before the pillar boxes came' sits correctly against the date; receiving houses at shop hatches are genuine pre-1852 practice; 'Michaelmas quarter' is a real accounting quarter; 'wanted a new spring' in the sense of 'needed' is period-correct. Threepence an hour is generous for the period and payment by the hour rather than by the letter is a fictional convenience, but it is stated as the town's rule and the passage stays consistent with it.

Two small things I noticed and cleared rather than flagged: (1) 'opened at seven in the morning and took in 412 letters' compresses a daily habit and a quarterly total into one clause, but the preceding sentence, 'The quarterly returns recorded the hours and the letters', licenses the quarterly reading, so the sentence resolves on first pass; (2) the aperture is a 'hatch' throughout and a 'flap' in the surveyor's note - a stylistic variation, not an inconsistency, since the flap is plausibly the moving part of the hatch. Neither cost me a re-read of the item, hence 'natural'.

'Governed' in D is a strong causal word for what is a two-shop comparison, but it is the only option the data can support, and the shared eight o'clock close is exactly the kind of hint an 'implied' stem asks a candidate to pick up.

Reads as authentic Swedish sakprosa of the popular-archaeology kind: concrete opening (spettet, motståndet som ändrar karaktär), then process, then a scholarly controversy, then an explicit 'det här vet vi inte' section, then a closing image. Paragraph function is clear throughout and I never had to reread a sentence to parse it.

Terminology is handled correctly and consistently: mossan (the moss) vs mossen (the bog) are kept apart; blästugn, lupp, räckning, varp, tappade kakor, rostbädd, tappgrop, mätts in are all real Swedish archaeometallurgical usage, and the four glossed terms are the ones a lay reader would actually need.

The metallurgy checks out: ~1200 grader melts the slag but not iron (which the text puts 'långt över 1500' - real value 1538); solid-state reduction with kolmonoxid drawing oxygen out of the ore grains; carburisation from harder blowing producing a more brittle bloom; low-iron (less fayalitic) slag being more viscous at bloomery temperatures. Nothing felt factually wrong to me.

Internal arithmetic hangs together across paragraphs: 'mer järn stannade i avfallet än som lämnade ugnen i luppen' is not asserted in a vacuum - it is corroborated later by 'en blåsning gav några kilo järn' against 'varpen räknas i ton'. Site counts are also consistent: 11 sampled furnace sites, 14 surveyed in the parish, 9 reconstructed furnaces, 36 firings.

Q1 (C): the passage says senhösten when the water had dropped, ore left out over the winter, 'Först därefter rostades den'. A inverts both season and order, B is contradicted by 'Långt ifrån varje mosse bär ett sådant skikt', D by 'Utan spettet gick skiktet inte att finna'.

Q2 (A): 'De blåsningar som drevs hårdast ... gav inte större luppar utan sprödare: kolet gick in i järnet'. B reverses the direction, C overstates ('samtliga misslyckades'), D names something the experiments are never said to have shown.

Reads as an authentic Swedish debattartikel: first-person recantation by a named board member ('Nu vill jag ta tillbaka min röst'), a declared conflict of interest ('Föreningen skulle dessutom ersättas för tillsynen, vilket borde ha gjort mig misstänksam mot min egen entusiasm'), a concession paragraph, a concrete counter-proposal ('Köp bojarna ... över driftsbudgeten'), and an anecdotal closing image. Register, idiom and vocabulary (oavkortat, remissvar, stridsfråga, landfästet, trallen, uppställningsrutor, tömningsstation, betalningsgrad om 31 procent, kastlina) are all correct and native-sounding; no calques or agreement errors spotted.
Arithmetic checks out: 4 800 betalda bad x 20 kr = 96 000 kr, correctly described as 'knappt hundratusen kronor per säsong'.

The argument is quantitatively coherent even though the text never spells the sum out: at the ställplats payment rate of 31 percent the brygga would yield ca 29 800 kr against 61 000 kr in equipment plus 9 000 kr annual tillsyn, so the 'sign-and-code' precedent really does undercut the förvaltning's calculation. Good that the reader can do this step without being led by the hand.

Incident distribution is internally consistent with the closing anecdote: 11 of 14 tillbud (79 percent) at Stångklippan, and 18 of 21 bathers counted (86 percent) up on the cliff. The self-limiting caveat ('Badvärdarna för visserligen dagbok bara under skolloven') is a realistic debate move and does not undermine the claim.

q:1 is a clean attitude/main-thesis question. D is the only option that holds both halves of the author's position ('Att åtgärder behövs är ingen stridsfråga' plus the fee objection). B is refuted by the cut line and the ladder ending half a metre above the water; C is the position she explicitly recants; A (higher fee) is nowhere in the text.

q:2 requires one genuine inference step, 31 percent paid -> ca 69 percent unpaid -> 'sju av tio nätter obetalda'. The rounding is honest (69 rounds to 7 of 10) and B/C/D are all cleanly excluded: the kommun's uppföljning did measure the rate, so B is false; C inverts it; D is unsupported.

Reads as an authentic Swedish essä: laconic first-person archive piece with a self-correction arc (suspicion -> evidence -> concession -> residual loose ends -> deflating factual coda). Period register is right and unforced: handlande/köpman/fabrikör as status-graded trade titles, hemmansägare, widows kept as "änka efter", a local telefonförening printing its own catalogues and later its "sista egna katalog 1949" (correctly implying the later Televerket takeover). Idiom is native throughout: "upptog" for "listed", "vare sig raden fylldes med ett ord eller med fem", "får jag ändå inte att gå ihop", correct V2 inversion in "I de fall där skriften gick att jämföra ... härrörde yrkesordet i regel från abonnenten själv". No calque, no seam between paragraphs, no wrong-feeling fact.

Architecture is tight and checkable: paragraph 2 names exactly three mechanisms (printed list of approved designations / fee penalising long titles / an opinionated kassör) and paragraph 4 refutes exactly those three in the same order (blank title row with no list or length instruction / same fee for one word or five, table reprinted unchanged 1919 and 1926 / handwriting shows the word came from the subscriber). "Ingen av mina tre mekanismer fanns alltså" therefore lands honestly.

Internal date/count cross-checks: eleven catalogues across 1907-1931 = ten intervals over 24 years = ~2.4 years, so "tillfället kom ungefär vartannat år" is a fair approximation. 1919 and 1926 both fall inside the studied span. The "elva kataloger" is scoped "mellan 1907 och 1931", so the later 1938 and 1949 catalogues create no contradiction. "Fyra uppgifter: nummer, namn, adress och yrke" reconciles with the post-1938 "tre kolumner: nummer, namn, adress".

One arithmetic point I paused on but do not treat as friction: first catalogue 14 handlande + 2 fabrikörer = 16 trade entries; last 3 + 9 + 11 = 23, i.e. +7 over 24 years. The sentence hedges this itself ("utan att särskilt många nya rörelser hade öppnat"), and the argument does not need equal totals — it needs the composition shift (14 handlande down to 3 while köpmän go 0->9), which the numbers do carry. A second soft point: "drygt trehundra" anmälningar "från hela perioden" is fewer forms than eleven refill rounds would have generated, but "låg kvar" plus the stem's "bevarade" plus "I de fall där skriften gick att jämföra" all signal a partial surviving archive, so it reconciles.

STEMS-AND-OPTIONS-ONLY (no passage) — this is a real leak, and it is worse in the pair than in either question alone. Q1 alone: I narrow 4 -> 2 and lean hard on D. A ("nedskrivna av föreningens egen kassör") and C ("blanketten räknade upp de yrkesbeteckningar som en abonnent hade rätt att välja mellan") are two variants of the same institutional-control claim, so under the no-two-equivalent-options convention both are suspect; B and C are flat absolutes while D alone carries two hedges ("i regel", "där skriften gick att jämföra"), the standard signature of the keyed option in this format. Blind, I commit D at roughly 70 percent. Q2 alone: weaker, 4 -> 2, a soft lean to B. The stem presupposes the author HAS a "misstanke" and option A names an "arkivarien" who exists only to be conceded to; the essay genre schema (writer investigates, is corrected, concedes) plus the harshness of "avfärdar arkivarien" pushes against A, and D ("båda förklaringarna behövs") is the usual synthesis decoy. Blind, B at roughly 55-60 percent. Q1+Q2 together is where it breaks: Q2/B's "godtar den VANLIGA förklaringen" tells you the author's own hypothesis lost, and Q1's option set tells you the author's hypothesis was institutional control (A/C), so the surviving Q1 answer must be the non-institutional one, D — and symmetrically Q1/D confirms Q2/B. Read as a pair, both go to roughly 80 percent with the passage unopened. Net: a test-wise candidate can plausibly bank both marks blind, so this unit is currently under-protected as a two-question set.

Contributing structural cause of the leak, if it is to be fixed: Q1's four options are effectively a mechanism inventory (kassör / correction / printed list / subscriber's own), which reprints the author's hypothesis space that the passage builds; and Q2's options are stances rather than content, so they inherit whatever Q1 discloses. Q2 is also the more solvable of the two once Q1 is read, which is the reverse of the intended dependency.
